content: Bruxism is characterized by repetitive, involuntary grinding and clenching of the teeth, which can occur during the day (diurnally) or at night (nocturnally). The term La Bruxomanie was first introduced in 1907 by Marie Pielkiewics, and the English term bruxism was coined in 1931 by Frohman. Bruxism is classified into two types: awake bruxism and sleep bruxism, depending on the individual's physiological sleep state. The etiology of bruxism is multifactorial and can be categorized into three groups: psychosocial factors, peripheral factors, and pathophysiological factors. It is believed to involve disturbances in brain neurotransmitters or the basal ganglia. Bruxism affects men and women equally. Risk factors for bruxism include obstructive sleep apnea, alcohol abuse, caffeine intake, smoking, and anxiety. Symptoms of bruxism often develop in childhood, typically during the first decade of life, and may begin with the eruption of the primary upper and lower anterior teeth. Common complications include tooth wear, tooth hypersensitivity, and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain. Bruxism is primarily diagnosed based on clinical presentation. The most common symptom is involuntary rhythmic contractions of the masticatory muscles during sleep. Secondary symptoms may include morning headaches, jaw pain, and clicking in the TMJ. Dental deformities such as tooth wear, thermal sensitivity, and hypermobility may also be observed. Severe cases can result in soft tissue injuries, dental fractures, difficulty chewing, and head and neck pain. The pathophysiology of bruxism involves reflex chewing activity, which is not a learned habit. Chewing is a complex neuromuscular activity controlled by reflex nerve pathways and higher brain centers. During sleep, the reflex component remains active while higher control is inactive, leading to bruxism. Imbalances in the basal ganglia's direct and indirect pathways, which coordinate movement, may contribute to bruxism. These imbalances are associated with disturbances in dopamine-mediated neurotransmission. Acute use of dopamine precursors like L-dopa can inhibit bruxism, while chronic use may exacerbate it. Long-term use of serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and substances like amphetamines and nicotine, which influence dopamine activity, have also been linked to bruxism. The arousal response, a sudden change in sleep depth accompanied by body movements, increased heart rate, respiratory changes, and muscle activity, has been studied as a potential cause of bruxism. Disturbances in the central neurotransmitter system may play a role in its etiology. Bruxism is one of the most common sleep disorders, affecting 30 to 40 million Americans. It can occur during short naps as well as prolonged sleep. It is more prevalent in individuals younger than six years of age, with incidence decreasing with age. Management of bruxism begins with the removal of any offending agents, such as medications or substances contributing to the condition. A wait-and-see approach is recommended for medication-induced bruxism, as spontaneous remission often occurs after cessation of the offending agent. Pharmacotherapy focuses on symptom alleviation, with buspirone (15–20 mg/day) and gabapentin (100–300 mg/day) being the preferred medications. Surgery is considered the mainstay of treatment in severe cases. In summary, bruxism is a multifactorial condition with a complex pathophysiology involving neurotransmitter imbalances and neuromuscular activity. While it is often mild and self-limiting, severe cases can lead to significant complications requiring medical or surgical intervention.
